questions: Did the unsteady walking begin suddenly, over minutes to hours?
Do you currently have weakness or numbness on one side of your body?
Do you have difficulty speaking, double vision, facial drooping, or trouble swallowing?
Do you have a severe or unusual headache?
Do you have severe dizziness or a spinning sensation?
Have you recently fallen or suffered a head injury?
Do you have fever, neck stiffness, or a new rash?
Have you recently consumed a large amount of alcohol or taken sedatives, sleeping pills, anticonvulsants, or other new medications?
Has the unsteadiness been progressively worsening over days, weeks, or months?
Do you have tremor, slurred speech, or clumsiness of your hands?
Do you have numbness or reduced awareness of the position of your feet?
Do you have hearing loss or ringing in either ear?
Do you have urinary difficulty, memory problems, or changes in thinking?
Have you had recurrent episodes of similar unsteadiness?
Do close relatives have a similar walking disorder or another inherited neurological condition?
Do you have a history of cancer, HIV, or another condition that weakens your immune system?
Do you have diabetes, thyroid disease, vitamin B12 deficiency, or significant malnutrition?
Have you recently had a gastrointestinal illness, respiratory infection, or vaccination?
Are you pregnant or could you be pregnant?
Is the unsteadiness worse when you close your eyes?

results: 1. Complete neurological examination, including ocular saccades and pursuit, nystagmus, dysarthria, limb coordination, heel-to-shin testing, gait, tandem gait, reflexes, and plantar responses
deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses: normal
coordination examination (limb and truncal): limb and truncal ataxia
3. MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium contrast
brain MRI: cerebellar atrophy on sagittal T1 and axial FLAIR
MRI brain with gadolinium: cerebellar atrophy without gadolinium enhancement
4. Serum vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, copper, vitamin E, and folate
copper / caeruloplasmin: normal - excludes Wilson disease
vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid: normal
6. Liver function tests, renal function tests, electrolytes, calcium, and glucose
serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine: normal
serum calcium, magnesium and phosphate: normal
7. Serum anti-GAD65, anti-Yo, anti-Hu, anti-Ri, and anti-amphiphysin antibodies
8. Cerebrospinal fluid examination with cell count, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands, IgG index, infectious studies, and paraneoplastic testing
lumbar puncture / CSF: normal cells, protein and glucose; no oligoclonal bands
CSF cell count and differential: normal
CSF oligoclonal bands and IgG index: normal
CSF culture and viral PCR: normal
9. Comprehensive hereditary spinocerebellar ataxia genetic panel, including repeat-expansion analysis for SCA1, SCA2, SCA3, SCA6, SCA7, SCA17, and FXTAS
genetic ataxia panel: 112 and 29 CTG repeats in ATXN8OS - confirms SCA8
11. Friedreich ataxia FXN GAA-repeat expansion testing
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 8 (SCA8), an autosomal-dominant ATXN8OS/ATXN8 CTG/CAG repeat-expansion disorder

ALTERNATIVE: RFC1 biallelic AAGGG repeat-expansion disease (late-onset cerebellar ataxia/CANVAS)

ALTERNATIVE: Friedreich ataxia due to biallelic FXN GAA-repeat expansions

ALTERNATIVE: Sporadic late-onset cerebellar ataxia (idiopathic degenerative cerebellar ataxia) despite the SCA8 expansion finding
order_raw:

3. MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium contrast

8. Cerebrospinal fluid examination with cell count, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands, IgG index, infectious studies, and paraneoplastic testing
9. Comprehensive hereditary spinocerebellar ataxia genetic panel, including repeat-expansion analysis for SCA1, SCA2, SCA3, SCA6, SCA7, SCA17, and FXTAS
10. RFC1 biallelic AAGGG repeat-expansion testing
11. Friedreich ataxia FXN GAA-repeat expansion testing

13. Formal neuropsychological assessment
